column1: the virtual-pipe model is described as having a depth-dependent signal speed, which is false for the constant cross-section every source actually specifies
column3: celerity rises with depth, so a filling pool gets progressively more expensive; recompute the limit from the current state every step
column4: Mei eq. (2) gives A as a pipe cross-section parameter with no depth dependence, and Stava sec. 4 eq. (1) is decisive: "In our simulation this area is always constant with profile C = l^2". Linearising gives signal speed sqrt(g*A/l) -- an EFFECTIVE depth set by A/l, not the water depth. With Stava's A = l^2 the grid sloshes like water one cell deep no matter how deep the pool is.
column5: Bisected critical dt with the clamp disabled: constant A=1 gives dt_crit 0.1604 at depths 0.1, 1.0 and 10 alike; A = h*lx gives 0.5056 / 0.1599 / 0.0506. The ratio dt_crit/(dx/sqrt(g*A/l)) held at 0.502 across A in {1,4}, l in {1,4}, dx in {1,2} and two decades of depth. Advective speed is not in the constant-A bound either: dt_crit moved only 0.1604 -> 0.1601 as background transport went 0 -> 50 m/s.
column6: corrected; the document now says which bound governs which formulation rather than printing one bound for both

column4: Wave Particles solves the plain second-order wave equation at a CONSTANT speed (its eq. 1), so it has no dispersion at all; its dispersion angle is a wavefront-spreading geometry term, not frequency dispersion. It is also not costly: 170 fps at 100 000 particles on 2007 hardware, and the paper says under 10 000 give nearly identical results. Emergent refraction and shoaling over a varying bed belong to the later wave-packet literature, which Gaia has not read.
column5: Read at cemyuksel.com/research/waveparticles/waveparticles.pdf. Eq. 1 is the constant-speed wave equation; sec. 3.2 says the wave speed is constant; sec. 3.3 defines boundaries as container edges; sec. 6 Table 1 and text give the timings; sec. 7 lists diffraction under future work.

column1: the epsilon fill's tie-breaking requirement is omitted, and a bare binary heap violates it
column3: open = min-priority-queue keyed on elevation, with no mention of how ties are resolved
column4: Barnes et al. 2014 Algorithm 3 (Priority-Flood+epsilon) opens with "Let Open be a priority queue WITH TOTAL ORDER". Sec 4 Ordering explains: with eps = 0 a total and a strict weak ordering "produce the same results", but once eps != 0 the total order is what guarantees each cell a shortest path to its flooding source, and hence that a depression with several equally-low outlets drains through the nearest. heapq, std::priority_queue and every plain binary heap are STRICT WEAK: equal keys emerge in whatever order internal swaps produced.
column5: Reproduced. Flat basin, two outlets at exactly equal elevation, epsilon fill, tie order randomised over six seeds: the FILLED SURFACE IS BIT-IDENTICAL every time, so nothing that checks elevations sees anything wrong. The drainage is what moves -- up to 13 of 361 interior cells change which outlet they flood from, and the basin's split wanders 181/180 to 187/174 across seeds. An earlier attempt with a FIFO-vs-LIFO tiebreak found no difference at all and was wrong to conclude from that: both of those are total orders, just different ones. Only genuinely arbitrary tie resolution exposes it.
column6: fixed; the block now requires a total order and says to push a monotonic counter, and the measurement is in the document

column1: our priority-flood block is Algorithm 1, while the paper's epsilon variant is built on Algorithm 2

Barnes' own Algorithm 3 is a variation of the IMPROVED Priority-Flood (Algorithm 2), which adds a plain FIFO queue for a depression's interior once its rim is known, so only m <= n cells reach the priority queue. Sec 5 Analysis gives the float bound as O(m log2 m), m <= n -- not the O(n log n) our block's every-cell-through-the-queue structure gives.
column5: Read in the arXiv PDF (1511.04463): Algorithm 2's header says "uses a plain queue to speed-up the filling of depressions, once they are found"; Sec 5 states the O(m log2 m) reduction for floating-point DEMs.
column6: fixed; both algorithms are now named, the bound corrected, and the fill is noted to be identical either way
